Laser engravers often advertise top speeds like 1,000 mm/s or 2,000 mm/s, but those values rarely reflect real engraving performance. This article explains the difference between advertised maximum speed, raster speed, vector speed, and real-time acceleration.

 

 

1. The Reality Behind Laser Processing Speeds

Maximum speed is a theoretical number — the laser head’s top motion speed without engraving complexity. In real applications, precision and material response reduce that value significantly.

 

2. Raster Engraving Speed — The Pace of Detail

Raster engraving scans the head back and forth like a printer. Actual speed depends on how fast the head can accelerate and decelerate at the start and end of each line. Acceleration, not just speed, determines output efficiency.

 

 

3. Vector Speed — Cutting and Outlining

Vector engraving follows defined paths and slows down at every curve or corner to maintain accuracy. A circle cuts faster than a square at the same speed because it has fewer sharp turns.

 

 

4. The Unsung Hero: Real-Time Acceleration

Acceleration defines how quickly the head reaches working speed. Higher acceleration = faster completion and better precision, avoiding overburns at corners.

 

 

5. Why Real-World Performance Matters More

Machines with higher acceleration outperform those with only high top speeds in most real engraving jobs. Look for acceleration rate (mm/s²), review real test results, and check engraving consistency.
